title: Second-largest value without sorting
prompt:
Write a function second_largest(numbers) that returns the second largest distinct value in a list of integers, without using sorted() or list.sort().

numbers: a list of integers; it may be empty and may contain duplicates and negative values.
Return: the second largest distinct integer, or None when the list contains fewer than two distinct values.

Examples:
second_largest([3, 1, 4, 4, 2]) returns 3
second_largest([10, 9, 8]) returns 9
second_largest([5, 5]) returns None

Edge cases: an empty list returns None; a single value returns None; duplicates of the maximum count as one value, so [5, 5, 4] returns 4; negative numbers behave normally, so [-3, -1, -2] returns -2.

tests.name: basic ordering
tests.code:
assert second_largest([3, 1, 4, 4, 2]) == 3
assert second_largest([10, 9, 8]) == 9
assert second_largest([0, 7, 3]) == 3

tests.name: fewer than two distinct values
tests.code:
assert second_largest([5, 5, 5]) is None
assert second_largest([1]) is None
assert second_largest([]) is None

tests.name: duplicates and negatives
tests.code:
assert second_largest([5, 5, 4]) == 4
assert second_largest([-3, -1, -2]) == -2
assert second_largest([10, -5, 10, -5, 7]) == 7

hints: Track the largest and the second largest value in a single pass.
When a new larger value appears, the old largest becomes the new second largest.
Skip values equal to the current largest so duplicates are not counted twice.

title: Recursively flatten nested lists
prompt:
Write a function flatten(nested) that takes a list whose elements are integers or other lists (nested to any depth) and returns a new one-dimensional list containing all integers in their original order.

nested: a list of integers and lists, arbitrarily nested. The input must not be modified.
Return: a new flat list of integers.

Examples:
flatten([1, 2, 3]) returns [1, 2, 3]
flatten([[1, 2], [3, [4, [5]]], []]) returns [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
flatten([]) returns []

Edge cases: empty inner lists contribute nothing; deep nesting such as [[[[7]]]] returns [7]; the original nested list stays unchanged.

tests.name: flat input and empty list
tests.code:
assert flatten([1, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3]
assert flatten([]) == []

tests.name: input is not modified
tests.code:
_original = [[1, 2], [3, [4]]]
_result = flatten(_original)
assert _result == [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert _original == [[1, 2], [3, [4]]]
assert flatten([[[7]]]) == [7]

hints: Handle one element at a time and recurse when the element is itself a list.
Collect integers into a list that you pass down or extend with recursive results.
An empty list simply contributes no elements.

title: Invert a dictionary, grouping duplicate values

tests.name: empty input and string values

hints: First group all original keys by their value, then decide how each group is stored.
A group with one key maps to that key; a larger group maps to the sorted keys.
Build a new dict instead of changing the input.

title: Greeting with default arguments
prompt:
Write a function greet(name, greeting="Hello", punctuation="!") that returns a greeting string.

name: the person's name (a string).
greeting: the opening word, default "Hello".
punctuation: the closing text, default "!".
Return: a string in the form "<greeting>, <name><punctuation>".

Examples:
greet("Ana") returns "Hello, Ana!"
greet("Ana", greeting="Hi") returns "Hi, Ana!"
greet("Ana", punctuation=".") returns "Hello, Ana."

Edge cases: both optional arguments can be passed by keyword together, so greet("Ana", greeting="Hey", punctuation="?") returns "Hey, Ana?"; positional arguments work too.

tests.name: default arguments
tests.code:
assert greet("Ana") == "Hello, Ana!"
assert greet("Bo") == "Hello, Bo!"

tests.name: overriding one default
tests.code:
assert greet("Ana", greeting="Hi") == "Hi, Ana!"
assert greet("Ana", punctuation=".") == "Hello, Ana."

tests.name: overriding both defaults
tests.code:
assert greet("Ana", greeting="Hey", punctuation="?") == "Hey, Ana?"
assert greet("Ana", "Salut", "...") == "Salut, Ana..."

solution:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello", punctuation="!"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}{punctuation}"
hints: Use default parameter values for greeting and punctuation.
Build the result with an f-string that places the comma and spaces exactly.
Keyword arguments let the caller skip greeting and set only punctuation.

title: Variable-argument sum with a starting value
prompt:
Write a function sum_all(*numbers, start=0) that adds any number of numeric positional arguments and returns the total, beginning from start.

numbers: zero or more ints or floats.
start: a keyword-only argument with default 0.
Return: start plus the sum of numbers; with no numbers the result equals start.

Examples:
sum_all() returns 0
sum_all(1, 2, 3) returns 6
sum_all(1.5, 2.5, start=10) returns 14.0

Edge cases: negative values are allowed; start is passed by keyword; sum_all(*range(101)) returns 5050.

tests.name: no arguments and one argument
tests.code:
assert sum_all() == 0
assert sum_all(5) == 5

tests.name: several numbers and a start
tests.code:
assert sum_all(1, 2, 3, 4) == 10
assert sum_all(1.5, 2.5, start=10) == 14.0
assert sum_all(-1, -2, start=10) == 7

tests.name: many arguments from an unpacked range
tests.code: assert sum_all(*range(101)) == 5050

solution:
def sum_all(*numbers, start=0):
    return start + sum(numbers)
hints: Collect the positional arguments with *numbers so any count is accepted.
Make start keyword-only by placing it after *numbers in the signature.
Add the built-in sum of the collected tuple to start.

title: Memoising wrapper function
prompt:
Write a function memoize(fn) that returns a new function which caches the results of fn.

fn: a function that accepts only positional arguments.
Return: a wrapper function. The first time the wrapper is called with a given tuple of positional arguments, it calls fn and stores the result; later calls with the same arguments return the stored result without calling fn again. The wrapper must return exactly what fn returns.

Examples:
double = memoize(lambda n: n * 2) then double(3) returns 6, and a second double(3) call does not call the lambda again.
fib = memoize(recursive_fib) then fib(15) returns 610 quickly because every intermediate result is cached.
memoize(lambda: 42)() returns 42 no matter how often it is called.

Edge cases: the wrapper may be called with no arguments; it must work for recursive functions that call themselves through the decorated name; different argument tuples are cached separately.

tests.name: caches repeated positional calls
tests.code:
_calls = []
def _double(n):
    _calls.append(n)
    return n * 2
_double = memoize(_double)
assert _double(3) == 6
assert _double(3) == 6
assert _calls == [3]
assert _double(4) == 8
assert _calls == [3, 4]

tests.name: works with a recursive function
function with no arguments
tests.code:
_constant_calls = []
def _constant():
    _constant_calls.append(1)
    return 42
_constant = memoize(_constant)
assert _constant() == 42
assert _constant() == 42
assert len(_constant_calls) == 1

hints: Keep a dictionary in the enclosing scope so every call of the wrapper shares it.
Build the cache key from the positional arguments tuple, which also covers a call with no arguments.
Only call fn when the key is missing, and always return the cached value.

title: Count vowels case-insensitively
prompt:
Write a function count_vowels(text) that counts how many vowels appear in text.

text: a string.
Return: an integer count of the letters a, e, i, o, u in either upper or lower case. Consonants, digits and punctuation are ignored.

Examples:
count_vowels("Hello World") returns 3
count_vowels("XYZ") returns 0
count_vowels("AEIOUaeiou") returns 10

Edge cases: the empty string returns 0; y is never counted as a vowel; digits and punctuation add nothing.

tests.name: mixed case text
tests.code:
assert count_vowels("Hello World") == 3
assert count_vowels("AEIOUaeiou") == 10

tests.name: no vowels
tests.code:
assert count_vowels("") == 0
assert count_vowels("XYZ") == 0
assert count_vowels("123 !?") == 0

tests.name: letters with y and mixed content
tests.code:
assert count_vowels("The quick brown fox") == 5
assert count_vowels("Rhythm") == 0

solution:
def count_vowels(text):
    return sum(1 for char in text.lower() if char in "aeiou")
hints: Lowercase the text once so you only need to check five letters.
A generator expression inside sum counts the matching characters.
Remember that y is not one of the five vowels.

title: Palindrome ignoring case and non-letters
prompt:
Write a function is_palindrome(text) that decides whether text reads the same forwards and backwards after removing every non-letter character and ignoring case.

text: a string.
Return: True or False. Keep only alphabetic characters (str.isalpha), lowercase them, and compare that sequence with its reverse.

Examples:
is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama") returns True
is_palindrome("race a car") returns False
is_palindrome("") returns True

Edge cases: a string without letters, such as "12321", is a palindrome because nothing remains; digits and punctuation are removed first, so "ab1ba" returns True and "ab1ca" returns False.

tests.name: classic palindromes
tests.code:
assert is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama") is True
assert is_palindrome("Was it a car or a cat I saw?") is True

tests.name: non-palindrome and empty string
tests.code:
assert is_palindrome("race a car") is False
assert is_palindrome("") is True

tests.name: digits are ignored
tests.code:
assert is_palindrome("12321") is True
assert is_palindrome("ab1ba") is True
assert is_palindrome("ab1ca") is False

hints: Filter the string down to letters with str.isalpha and lowercase each one.
Compare the resulting list with its reverse using slicing.
An empty letters list is equal to its reverse, so it counts as a palindrome.

title: Right-align a table of numbers
prompt:
Write a function format_table(rows) that renders a rectangular table of integers as plain text with right-aligned columns.

rows: a list of equal-length lists of integers; it may be empty.
Return: a string with one line per row. Each cell is converted to text and padded on the left with spaces until it is as wide as the widest cell in its column; columns are separated by exactly one space; lines are separated by a single newline character (no trailing newline). An empty rows list returns the empty string.

Examples:
format_table([[1, 20], [300, 4]]) returns "  1 20\n300  4"
format_table([[7, 88, 9]]) returns "7 88 9"
format_table([]) returns ""

Edge cases: negative numbers include their minus sign when measuring width; a single-cell table such as [[5]] returns "5"; lines never end with trailing spaces.

tests.name: single row, single cell and empty table
tests.code:
assert format_table([[7, 88, 9]]) == "7 88 9"
assert format_table([[5]]) == "5"
assert format_table([]) == ""

hints: First compute the widest text in each column by indexing the rows.
Right-align every cell with str.rjust using that column width.
Join cells with one space and join lines with a newline, and handle the empty table before indexing rows[0].

title: Convert to int with a fallback
prompt:
Write a function safe_int(value, default=0) that converts value to an integer and returns default when the conversion fails.

value: any value.
default: the fallback value, 0 by default.
Return: int(value) when the conversion succeeds, otherwise default. Catch only ValueError and TypeError so unrelated errors are not hidden.

Examples:
safe_int("42") returns 42
safe_int("abc") returns 0
safe_int(None, -1) returns -1

Edge cases: safe_int(" 7 ") returns 7 because int() ignores surrounding whitespace; safe_int("3.5") returns the default because "3.5" is not a valid integer literal; safe_int(3.9) returns 3 because int() truncates a float.

tests.name: successful conversions
tests.code:
assert safe_int("42") == 42
assert safe_int(" 7 ") == 7
assert safe_int(-5) == -5

tests.name: failed conversions fall back
tests.code:
assert safe_int("abc") == 0
assert safe_int(None, -1) == -1
assert safe_int("3.5") == 0
assert safe_int("abc", default=9) == 9

tests.name: float truncation and bad types
tests.code:
assert safe_int(3.9) == 3
assert safe_int([], 100) == 100
assert safe_int("0") == 0

hints: Put int(value) inside a try block and return the converted value.
Catch ValueError for bad strings and TypeError for values int() cannot accept.
Return default from the except branch instead of letting the error escape.

title: Retry a call once
prompt:
Write a function retry_once(func, *args, **kwargs) that calls func(*args, **kwargs) and, if that call raises an Exception, calls it exactly once more with the same arguments.

func: any callable.
args, kwargs: positional and keyword arguments forwarded unchanged to func.
Return: the return value of the successful call. If the first call succeeds, func must not be called again. If the second call raises, that second exception propagates unchanged.

Examples:
retry_once(lambda x: x, 5) returns 5
a function that raises on its first call and returns "ok" on its second call makes retry_once return "ok"
a function that always raises ValueError("nope") makes retry_once raise ValueError("nope") after exactly two calls

Edge cases: only Exception subclasses trigger a retry; keyword arguments must be forwarded correctly; there is exactly one retry, never a third attempt.

tests.name: first call succeeds
tests.code:
_identity_calls = []
def _identity(x):
    _identity_calls.append(x)
    return x
assert retry_once(_identity, 5) == 5
assert _identity_calls == [5]
def _add(a, b=0):
    return a + b
assert retry_once(_add, 1, b=2) == 3

tests.name: first call fails then succeeds
tests.code:
_flaky_calls = []
def _flaky():
    _flaky_calls.append(1)
    if len(_flaky_calls) < 2:
        raise RuntimeError("boom")
    return "ok"
assert retry_once(_flaky) == "ok"
assert len(_flaky_calls) == 2

tests.name: second failure propagates

hints: Wrap only the first call in try/except and return its result immediately when it succeeds.
In the except branch call func again with the same forwarded arguments.
Let the second call run outside the try so its exception propagates unchanged.

title: Custom exception hierarchy and lookup
prompt:
Define a small exception hierarchy and a lookup function.

Define these classes:
class AppError(Exception) is the base class for application errors.
class NotFoundError(AppError) is raised when a requested key is missing.
class InvalidInputError(AppError) is raised when the key has the wrong type.

Write a function lookup(mapping, key):
mapping: a dict with string keys.
key: the key to look up.
Return: mapping[key] when the key is present.
Raise InvalidInputError("key must be a string") when key is not a str.
Raise NotFoundError("missing key: " + key) when key is a str but absent from mapping.

Examples:
lookup({"a": 1}, "a") returns 1
lookup({"a": 1}, "b") raises NotFoundError with the message "missing key: b"
lookup({"a": 1}, 3) raises InvalidInputError with the message "key must be a string"

Edge cases: both custom errors must be catchable as AppError and as Exception; check the key type before the membership test so a non-string key always raises InvalidInputError; an empty dict with a string key raises NotFoundError.

tests.name: hierarchy and successful lookup
tests.code:
assert issubclass(AppError, Exception)
assert issubclass(NotFoundError, AppError)
assert issubclass(InvalidInputError, AppError)
assert lookup({"a": 1}, "a") == 1

tests.name: missing key
invalid key type

hints: Subclass both specific errors from AppError so one except clause can catch both.
Test isinstance(key, str) before checking membership, so wrong types never reach the dict lookup.
Raise the custom errors with exactly the documented message strings.

title: Count lines in a text file
prompt:
Write a function count_lines(path) that returns the number of lines in a UTF-8 text file.

path: a file system path, given as a str or a pathlib.Path.
Return: the number of lines. A final line without a trailing newline still counts as one line, and an empty file has 0 lines.

Examples:
a file containing "alpha", "beta", "gamma" on three lines without a trailing newline gives count_lines(path) == 3
a file containing "a\nb\n" gives 2
an empty file gives 0

Edge cases: a file containing only a single newline has one empty line and gives 1; open the file with a with statement and pass encoding="utf-8" so non-ASCII text works.

tests.name: three lines without a final newline
tests.code:
import tempfile, pathlib, shutil
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
try:
    _p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "sample.txt"
    _p.write_text("alpha\nbeta\ngamma", encoding="utf-8")
    _as_path = count_lines(_p)
    _as_str = count_lines(str(_p))
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(_tmp)
assert _as_path == 3
assert _as_str == 3

tests.name: trailing newline and empty file
tests.code:
import tempfile, pathlib, shutil
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
try:
    _p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "trailing.txt"
    _p.write_text("a\nb\n", encoding="utf-8")
    _trailing = count_lines(_p)
    _q = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "empty.txt"
    _q.write_text("", encoding="utf-8")
    _empty = count_lines(_q)
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(_tmp)
assert _trailing == 2
assert _empty == 0

tests.name: single blank line and non-ASCII text
tests.code:
import tempfile, pathlib, shutil
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
try:
    _p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "blank.txt"
    _p.write_text("\n", encoding="utf-8")
    _one = count_lines(_p)
    _q = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "unicode.txt"
    _q.write_text("h\u00e9llo\nw\u00f6rld", encoding="utf-8")
    _two = count_lines(_q)
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(_tmp)
assert _one == 1
assert _two == 2

hints: Open the path with a with statement and encoding='utf-8'.
Iterating over an open text file yields one string per line, including the last line without a newline.
Count the yielded lines with sum(1 for _ in handle).

title: Write and read back a list of lines
prompt:
Write two functions that store a list of strings in a text file and read it back.

write_lines(path, lines):
path: a file system path (str or pathlib.Path), overwritten if it exists.
lines: a list of strings.
Write each string followed by a single newline to a UTF-8 text file, in order. An empty list creates an empty file. Return None.

read_lines(path):
path: a file system path (str or pathlib.Path).
Return the file's lines as strings with the trailing newline removed. A final line without a newline is included as-is. An empty file returns [].

Examples:
write_lines(path, ["alpha", "beta"]) then path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") returns "alpha\nbeta\n" and read_lines(path) returns ["alpha", "beta"]
write_lines(path, []) then read_lines(path) returns []

Edge cases: blank lines are preserved, so ["a", "", "b"] round-trips as ["a", "", "b"]; non-ASCII text must survive; write_lines overwrites previous content; use a with statement and encoding="utf-8".

tests.name: write then read back
tests.code:
import tempfile, pathlib, shutil
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
try:
    _p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "lines.txt"
    write_lines(_p, ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"])
    _content = _p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    _back = read_lines(_p)
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(_tmp)
assert _content == "alpha\nbeta\ngamma\n"
assert _back == ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]

tests.name: empty list and blank lines
tests.code:
import tempfile, pathlib, shutil
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
try:
    _p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "lines.txt"
    write_lines(_p, [])
    _empty_content = _p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    _empty_back = read_lines(_p)
    write_lines(_p, ["a", "", "b"])
    _blank_back = read_lines(_p)
    _blank_content = _p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(_tmp)
assert _empty_content == ""
assert _empty_back == []
assert _blank_back == ["a", "", "b"]
assert _blank_content == "a\n\nb\n"

tests.name: overwrite, unicode and missing final newline
tests.code:
import tempfile, pathlib, shutil
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
try:
    _p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "lines.txt"
    _p.write_text("old\ncontent\n", encoding="utf-8")
    write_lines(_p, ["h\u00e9llo", "w\u00f6rld"])
    _unicode = read_lines(_p)
    _p.write_text("no-newline", encoding="utf-8")
    _last = read_lines(str(_p))
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(_tmp)
assert _unicode == ["h\u00e9llo", "w\u00f6rld"]
assert _last == ["no-newline"]

hints: Open the file once per function with a with statement and encoding='utf-8'.
In write_lines, append a newline to every string so an empty file has no stray newline.
In read_lines, drop one trailing newline from each line and keep the last line when it has none.

title: Sum a CSV column by header name
prompt:
Write a function sum_csv_column(path, column) that reads a CSV file with a header row and returns the sum of the numbers in one named column.

path: a file system path (str or pathlib.Path) to a UTF-8 CSV file.
column: the header name of the column to sum (a string).
Return: the total as a float. Empty cells count as 0. Values may be integers or decimals such as 1.5.
Raise KeyError when the header row does not contain column.

Examples:
A file whose content is:
name,amount
alpha,1.5
beta,2
gamma,3.5
gives sum_csv_column(path, "amount") == 7.0
A file with data rows where "alpha, inc" is a quoted name with amount 1.5, beta has an empty amount, and gamma has 2.5 gives sum_csv_column(path, "amount") == 4.0
A file with header name,amount makes sum_csv_column(path, "missing") raise KeyError

Edge cases: use the csv module (csv.DictReader) so quoted fields containing commas parse correctly; a file with only a header row returns 0.0; open the file with encoding="utf-8" and newline="".

tests.name: basic numeric column
tests.code:
import tempfile, pathlib, shutil
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
try:
    _p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "data.csv"
    _p.write_text("name,amount\nalpha,1.5\nbeta,2\ngamma,3.5\n", encoding="utf-8")
    _total = sum_csv_column(_p, "amount")
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(_tmp)
assert _total == 7.0

tests.name: quoted comma and empty cell
tests.code:
import tempfile, pathlib, shutil
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
try:
    _p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "data.csv"
    _p.write_text('name,amount\n"alpha, inc",1.5\nbeta,\ngamma,2.5\n', encoding="utf-8")
    _total = sum_csv_column(str(_p), "amount")
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(_tmp)
assert _total == 4.0

tests.name: header only and missing column
tests.code:
import tempfile, pathlib, shutil
_tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
try:
    _empty_p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "empty.csv"
    _empty_p.write_text("name,amount\n", encoding="utf-8")
    _zero = sum_csv_column(_empty_p, "amount")
    _data_p = pathlib.Path(_tmp) / "data.csv"
    _data_p.write_text("name,amount\nalpha,1\n", encoding="utf-8")
    try:
        sum_csv_column(_data_p, "missing")
    except KeyError:
        _raised = True
    else:
        _raised = False
finally:
    shutil.rmtree(_tmp)
assert _zero == 0.0
assert _raised is True

hints: Open the file with newline='' and pass it to csv.DictReader so the header names become keys.
Check reader.fieldnames before looping and raise KeyError when the column is absent.
Skip empty cells and add float(cell) for the rest, returning 0.0 for a header-only file.
